newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea criticises U.S. over ties with Seoul.
newsitem.headline: North Korea criticises U.S. over ties with Seoul.

text.p: North Korea on Saturday criticised the United States for reaffirming its alliance with South Korea, calling it an "anachronistic policy against detente".

Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) was reacting to a visit to South Korea last week by Washington's top official for Asia, Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord, who assured Seoul of continued U.S. backing after recent North-South clashes.

In a report monitored in Tokyo, KCNA said the U.S. position was not in accord with the spirit of an agreed framework for the improvement of U.S.-North Korean relations and would lead to the creation of "artificial obstacles" to the progress of the relationship.
It called the U.S. move "a hostile act posing an open threat" to North Korea "and a bellicose outcry to lead the phase of confrontation to the outbreak of war on the Korean peninsula."
It accused the United States of continuing to ship war supplies to South Korea and escalating war exercises with the South while encouraging Seoul in inter-Korean confrontation.
"While doing so, it talks in the international arena as if it were interested in peace on the Korean peninsula," it added.
"The United States must be mindful that our people and people's army will never pardon any act of encroaching upon their sovereignty but mete out a thousandfold punishment."
KCNA accused the United States of a using an incident last month in which a North Korean submarine went aground in South Korea as a pretext to deploy more weapons in the South.
Seoul says 26 North Koreans landed from the submarine and 22 have been killed by South Korean troops or found dead. One was captured and three are still missing.

In Seoul last week, Lord and South Korean Foreign Minister Gong Ro-myung agreed that the incident should not threaten a proposal for peace talks with North Korea. Seoul also pledged it would continue to support a nuclear pact with Pyongyang.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam have proposed four-party talks, including China, to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War with a permanent peace arrangement.

After the submarine incident, Seoul hinted it might withdraw its backing for the nuclear accord, under which Pyongyang agreed to scrap a programme the United States suspects was being used to make nuclear weapons, in return for two light water reactors to be supplied by South Korea.
